title: Opening the Gateway to Oral Participation https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.3102/00028312241278585
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), February 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page covers Mundelsee and Jurkowski's study of what helps shy middle-school students raise their hands and participate orally, using hand-raising as the key indicator of engagement. The researchers examined student-teacher relationships, peer relationships, and instructional techniques including warm calling and wait time, finding that supportive teacher relationships and warm calling both increase hand-raising among shy students, while stronger peer relationships can actually decrease it. The summary highlights a double-edged finding: very close student-teacher relationships can backfire, since students may feel the teacher already accepts their silence, softening the push to participate. Positive peer relationships carry a similar risk, as shy students may avoid raising their hands for fear of jeopardizing their social standing by standing out. Wait time and smaller class sizes both help by giving students time to formulate answers and reducing uncertainty, though smaller classes also raise the odds of being called on, which can increase anxiety for the most shy students.
points: Warm calling — calling on students in a supportive, low-threat way — increases hand-raising in highly shy students and is one of the study's clearest actionable levers.
Very close student-teacher relationships can paradoxically reduce participation, because students may sense the teacher already accepts their silence and no longer feel the pull to speak up.
Positive peer relationships can also suppress participation, since shy students may avoid raising their hand for fear of jeopardizing their social standing by standing out from friends.
Wait time helps shy students formulate answers and reduces their uncertainty before raising a hand, making it a low-cost, high-value classroom habit.
quotes: This research explores how to encourage shy middle school students to participate more in class.

The findings indicate that supportive teacher relationships and the use of warm calling can facilitate hand-raising for shy students, while better peer relationships may correlate with decreased hand-raising.
Teachers sometimes attribute a lack of interest or motivation to shy students, underestimating their abilities.
A good student-teacher relationship can encourage shy students to participate, but very close relationships may weaken this effect, as students may feel the teacher accepts their reticence.
Teachers' predominant use of warm calling strategies can increase shy students' safety and, thus, their hand raising.
Both social relatedness and instructional factors can promote hand raising in highly shy students, opening the gateway to their oral participation
